about: Overview

Every vehicle used on a road or other public place in the UK must have at least third party insurance. Using a vehicle without it, or allowing someone else to do so, is an offence under section 143 of the Road Traffic Act 1988. It is often recorded on a licence as an IN10.

No insurance cases are more common than many people expect, and a large number involve drivers who honestly believed they were covered. A policy may have been cancelled after a missed payment. A driver may have assumed their own policy let them drive a friend's car. A delivery driver may not have realised their cover did not include work for a food delivery app. An employee may have been told by their employer that a company van was insured when it was not.

The offence is one of strict liability. That means the prosecution does not have to prove that you knew you were uninsured. If you were driving and there was no valid policy covering that use, the offence is usually committed. What you believed and why can still matter a great deal, but it tends to matter in different ways, such as through special reasons or a specific statutory defence.

The consequences can be significant. Six to eight penalty points or a ban, a fine, the possible loss of the vehicle through police seizure and much higher insurance premiums in future. For new drivers, a conviction will normally lead to their licence being revoked.

The offence

The law on motor insurance is short, but the way it applies to real policies can be complicated. A solicitor will usually start by looking at exactly what the policy said and what the vehicle was being used for at the time.

The offence can be committed by the person driving, and also by someone who causes or permits another person to drive without insurance. A vehicle owner who lets a friend borrow the car without checking they are covered can face the same charge and the same penalties as the driver.

Once the prosecution shows that you were using the vehicle, it is usually for you to prove that you had valid insurance for that use. This is unusual in criminal law. In practice it means the policy documents, schedule and certificate are central to the case.

about.h3: The use matters as much as the policy

about: A policy covers certain drivers, a certain vehicle and certain types of use. If any of these did not match what was happening at the time, the driver may not have been insured even though a policy existed. Examples include using a car for commuting on a policy limited to social use, or carrying passengers or goods for payment without the right cover.

There is a specific defence for employees. Broadly, it can apply where the vehicle did not belong to the driver and was not hired or lent to them, they were using it in the course of their employment, and they did not know and had no reason to believe that it was uninsured. The details matter, and a solicitor will check whether each part applies.

Separately from driving, the registered keeper of a vehicle must keep it insured unless it has been declared off the road with a SORN. This is known as continuous insurance enforcement. It is usually dealt with through letters and penalties from the authorities rather than through the courts and points, but it can lead to prosecution if ignored.
Common situations
Many no insurance cases follow a familiar pattern. These are some of the situations that solicitors see most often. Each turns on its own facts and documents.

Some policies used to include cover for driving other people's cars, usually third party only. Many policies no longer include it, and where it does exist it is often limited. It may only apply to certain drivers, may exclude cars that you own or that are registered to you, and may not apply if your own car is off the road. Drivers often discover these limits only after being stopped.

A policy can be cancelled for reasons such as a missed payment, a failure to send documents the insurer asked for or a disagreement about information given when the policy was taken out. Insurers normally have to follow their own terms when cancelling, and the dates and notices involved can be important. A solicitor will look at what the insurer sent and when.

Driving for a delivery platform, running a taxi or carrying goods for payment usually needs specific cover. A standard social and commuting policy will not normally cover this. Business use policies also vary, and a solicitor will check whether the use at the time fell within the policy wording.

Employees sometimes drive vans or cars provided by their employer on the understanding that the business has arranged cover. If it has not, the employee may be able to rely on the employee defence or argue special reasons, while the employer may face a charge of permitting.

Problems also arise when someone buys a new car and assumes their old policy transfers automatically, when the registration number on the policy is wrong, or when a policy starts later in the day than the driver realised. Learner drivers practising in a family car without the right cover are another common situation.

Sometimes a parent insures a car as the main driver when a younger family member is really the main user. Insurers may treat this as giving them wrong information, which can affect whether the policy pays out and, in some cases, its validity. The criminal and insurance consequences can be complex, and a solicitor will look closely at the policy and what the insurer has said.
Court process
Driving without insurance is a summary offence, heard in the magistrates' court. The outline below explains how cases usually progress. A solicitor will explain what applies to your case.

Insurance cases often turn on documents rather than on disputed accounts of driving. Getting the right documents early can make a real difference. This might include the full policy wording, the certificate, the statement of fact given when the policy was taken out, payment records and any correspondence from the insurer.

Many cases start when the police check a vehicle against the Motor Insurance Database, often using number plate recognition cameras. If no insurance is shown, the driver may be asked to produce documents, given a fixed penalty or reported for prosecution. The vehicle may also be seized.

In some cases the police offer a fixed penalty with points instead of a prosecution. This is not available in every case and depends on the circumstances. A fixed penalty avoids court but means accepting the points. If no fixed penalty is offered, or it is not accepted, the case goes to court.

Prosecution may begin with a Single Justice Procedure notice, which asks for a written plea within 21 days, or with a summons or postal requisition to attend court. The time limits for bringing insurance prosecutions work differently from many other minor offences, so a case can start some time after the incident.

If you plead guilty, the court will consider any mitigation and decide the sentence. If you intend to argue special reasons, the court will usually hear evidence about them before sentencing. If you plead not guilty, for example because you say you were insured or rely on the employee defence, a trial date is set.

At trial, the court hears evidence about the use of the vehicle and the insurance position. Policy documents and evidence from the insurer may be needed. A special reasons hearing is similar in that you give evidence about the circumstances and the court decides whether they justify not giving points.
If convicted, the court decides the points or ban and the fine. You can appeal to the Crown Court within a short time limit if you think the decision was wrong.
Penalties
The penalties for driving without insurance are designed to make it a serious matter, because victims of uninsured drivers can otherwise be left without compensation.

The penalty also depends on whether there are other offences from the same incident, such as driving otherwise than in accordance with a licence. Where several offences are dealt with together, the court looks at the overall picture when deciding points and fines.

If you are convicted, the court must either endorse your licence with 6 to 8 penalty points or disqualify you. The court decides which based on the circumstances, such as how long the vehicle was uninsured, why and whether there was any accident. Points usually stay on your record for four years.

The court will usually impose a fine based on your income and the seriousness of the offence. The court may also take into account any money saved by not paying for insurance. You will also usually pay prosecution costs and a victim surcharge.

If the court accepts that there are special reasons, it can decide not to give points at all. Special reasons must relate to the circumstances of the offence, not to the effect of points on you. A common example is where the driver was genuinely misled about their cover by someone they were entitled to rely on. Even where special reasons are found, the court can still impose a fine.

Six or more points can trigger a totting up ban if they take your total to 12 or more within three years. A driver within two years of passing their test who receives six or more points will have their licence revoked by the DVLA and must retake their tests. This makes special reasons especially important for new drivers.

The police have power to seize a vehicle being driven without insurance. To get it back, the owner usually has to show valid insurance and pay release and storage charges. If it is not collected within the set period, it can be disposed of. These charges are separate from any court penalty.

If an uninsured driver causes an accident, the Motor Insurers' Bureau may compensate the victim and then try to recover the money from the driver. This is a civil matter, separate from the prosecution, and a solicitor can explain how it might affect you.
Costs
Costs in a no insurance case depend mainly on whether you plead guilty, argue special reasons or go to trial.

Many motoring firms offer fixed fees for a guilty plea with mitigation, a special reasons hearing, an exceptional hardship argument or a full trial. Special reasons and trials need more preparation, such as obtaining policy documents, statements and sometimes evidence from the insurer or employer. Ask the firm what each option involves and costs before you decide.

Driving without insurance does not carry a prison sentence, so legal aid for court is rarely granted. Most people pay privately. Some motor or home insurance policies include legal expenses cover, so it is worth checking your documents.

If your vehicle was seized, the release and storage charges are payable to recover it and continue to rise the longer it is held. These amounts are set by regulations and can change, so check the current figures with the police force or storage provider.

An IN10 conviction can increase insurance premiums significantly for several years, and some insurers may not offer cover at all. A solicitor can explain how different outcomes, such as points compared with special reasons, may affect this.

faqs: The offence
What does driving without insurance cover?

It covers using a vehicle on a road or other public place without a policy that covers that driver, that vehicle and that type of use. It also covers causing or permitting someone else to do so. So an owner who lends their car to someone who is not insured can face the same charge as the driver.
I thought I was insured. Is that a defence?

Usually not on its own, because the offence is one of strict liability. However, a genuine and reasonable belief that you were insured may support an argument for special reasons, which can allow the court not to give points. If you were an employee driving a work vehicle, a specific defence may apply. A solicitor will look at the facts.
Who has to prove I was insured?

In most cases it is for the driver to prove that there was a valid policy covering that use. That is why your policy documents, certificate and schedule are so important. If you say you were insured, gather everything you can and give it to your solicitor as early as possible.
What is the employee defence?

It is a statutory defence for some employees. It can apply where the vehicle did not belong to you and was not hired or lent to you, you were driving it in the course of your employment, and you did not know and had no reason to believe it was uninsured. Each part must be shown, and a solicitor can check whether your situation fits.
Can the vehicle owner be prosecuted too?

Yes. A person who causes or permits someone else to use a vehicle without insurance can be prosecuted, and the penalties are the same as for the driver. This often arises where a car is lent to a friend or family member, or where an employer allows staff to drive a vehicle that is not properly insured.
How long after the incident can I be prosecuted?

Insurance offences have different time limits from many other minor motoring offences. This can allow a prosecution to start some time after the incident, particularly where it took a while for the authorities to obtain the evidence. A solicitor can check whether your case was brought within the time allowed.
Does it matter that I was only driving a short distance?

The offence can be committed over any distance, even moving a car a few metres on a public road. However, in some cases the distance driven and the reason for driving, such as a genuine emergency, may be relevant to whether special reasons exist or to the penalty. A solicitor can explain how courts tend to view the circumstances in your case.
Policies and cover
Does my policy let me drive other cars?

Some policies include driving other cars cover, but many do not, and where it is included it is often limited to third party cover for certain drivers. It may not apply to cars you own or that are registered to you. Check your certificate and policy wording. A solicitor can look at the exact terms if you have been charged.
My insurer cancelled my policy without telling me. What then?

Insurers usually have to follow the cancellation terms in the policy, including giving notice. Whether you were insured on the day depends on the dates and what the insurer did. Ask the insurer for copies of any cancellation letters and when they were sent. A solicitor can review these and explain how they affect your case.
Is food delivery covered by my normal insurance?

Usually not. Delivering food or parcels for payment normally needs specific cover, often described as hire and reward or delivery cover. Standard social, domestic and commuting policies will not usually cover it. If you were stopped while working for a delivery platform, a solicitor will check your policy and any cover the platform provides.
I had just bought the car. Was I covered?

Insurance does not usually transfer automatically from one car to another. Some policies give short temporary cover for a newly bought vehicle, but many do not. Whether you were covered depends on your policy and what you told your insurer. A solicitor can look at the documents to see whether a defence or special reasons might apply.
What is the Motor Insurance Database?

It is the central record of insured vehicles in the UK. The police use it, often through number plate recognition cameras, to check whether a vehicle is insured. The database can occasionally be out of date or wrong. If you were insured but the database said otherwise, keep your certificate and contact your insurer to correct it.
What is continuous insurance enforcement?

It is the rule that the registered keeper must keep a vehicle insured unless it has been declared off the road with a SORN. The authorities compare vehicle records with insurance records and send letters to keepers of vehicles that appear uninsured. It is a separate matter from driving without insurance, and usually dealt with through penalties rather than points.
Is a learner driver covered by the family car insurance?

Not automatically. A learner usually needs to be named on the policy or have separate learner driver insurance, and must meet the conditions for supervised driving. If a learner was driving without the right cover, both the learner and the person who allowed them to drive could face charges. A solicitor can look at the policy and the circumstances.
Court and penalties
How many points will I get?

If you are convicted and not disqualified, the court must give between 6 and 8 points. The number depends on the circumstances, such as how long the vehicle was uninsured and why. The court can disqualify you instead of giving points. If special reasons are found, the court can decide not to give any points at all.
What are special reasons?

Special reasons are facts connected with the offence that can justify the court not endorsing your licence. In insurance cases a common example is being genuinely misled about your cover by someone you were entitled to rely on, such as your employer. Special reasons must be proved with evidence, usually at a hearing where you give evidence.
Do I have to go to court?

If you receive a Single Justice Procedure notice, you can respond in writing. If you want to argue special reasons or plead not guilty, the case will usually go to a court hearing, and you will normally need to attend to give evidence. Your solicitor will tell you when you need to be there.
Can I be offered a fixed penalty?

In some cases the police offer a fixed penalty with points instead of prosecution. This depends on the circumstances and is at the discretion of the police. Accepting it means taking the points without going to court. If you think you have special reasons or a defence, a solicitor can explain whether going to court might be worth considering.
I am a new driver. Will I lose my licence?

If you are within two years of passing your test, six or more points will lead the DVLA to revoke your licence. As an IN10 carries at least six points, a conviction will usually have that effect unless the court disqualifies you instead or finds special reasons not to endorse. You would then need to retake your theory and practical tests.
Can I appeal?

You can appeal to the Crown Court against conviction or sentence. Time limits are short, usually 21 days from sentence. If you were convicted without knowing about the case, there may be other ways to reopen it. A solicitor can explain your options and the risks involved.
Could I be banned instead of getting points?

Yes. The court can choose to disqualify you instead of endorsing your licence with points. This is more likely where the offence is serious, for example where a vehicle was used without insurance for a long time or there was an accident. Some drivers who would otherwise face a totting up ban or revocation ask the court to consider a short ban instead, and the court decides whether that is appropriate.
Your vehicle
The police seized my car. How do I get it back?

You will usually need to show that you are the owner or keeper, show valid insurance for the vehicle and pay the release and storage charges. The police or storage provider can tell you the current charges and deadline. If the vehicle is not claimed in time it may be disposed of, so act quickly.
Can I get the seizure charges back?

Usually only in limited circumstances, such as where the seizure was not lawful. Even if you later show you had a defence to the charge, recovering seizure costs is not straightforward. A solicitor can look at how the seizure happened and explain whether there is any basis for challenging it.
What if I had an accident while uninsured?

The victim may be compensated by the Motor Insurers' Bureau, which may then seek to recover the money from you personally. This is separate from the criminal case. Tell your solicitor about any accident, as it affects how serious the court considers the offence to be and may raise other issues.
Will a conviction affect my future insurance?

Yes. Insurers treat no insurance convictions seriously and premiums often rise substantially for several years. Some insurers may decline to offer cover. You must declare convictions when asked. Specialist brokers may be able to help find cover after a conviction.
Getting help
What documents should I gather?

Gather your certificate of insurance, policy schedule and wording, any letters or emails from your insurer, bank statements showing premium payments, and any messages from your employer or the vehicle owner about cover. Bring your court papers and any seizure paperwork too. These documents are often the heart of the case.
Will the solicitor contact my insurer?

The solicitor may need information from your insurer, such as the policy terms or cancellation letters. They can tell you how best to obtain it. Some insurers will only release information to the policyholder, so your help may be needed.
What will the solicitor ask me?

Expect questions about where you were going, why you were driving that vehicle, what you believed about the insurance and why, who told you what, and your driving record. If you drive for work, they will ask about your job. Honest and complete answers help the solicitor see whether a defence or special reasons might apply.
Is Leaflegal a law firm?

No. Leaflegal is an introduction service and does not give legal advice. We introduce you to one regulated law firm that handles motoring offences, and any advice comes from them. You decide whether to instruct the firm.
